title: Count What You Have
content:
What problem does this solve?
The clerk should not manually recount every name or write every roster number. Python can measure a collection and generate a predictable sequence of numbers.

Previously in your program
Departure needs a guide, enough supplies, and no active warning. Which expression approves departure?
  has_guide and supplies >= 10 and not warning_active
A version that uses or, or that forgets not, clears the wrong expeditions.

Basic syntax
  len(party)
  for number in range(1, len(party) + 1):
      print(number)
  for index in range(len(party)):
      print(index, party[index])

What actually happens
len(value) returns how many items are present. It works on lists and strings, but counts different things: list items versus characters. range(stop) begins at 0 and stops before stop. range(start, stop) uses an explicit start and still excludes the stop. range(len(party)) produces valid list indexes. For human-facing numbering, range(1, len(party) + 1) produces 1 through the party size.

When this is useful
Use len to measure, and range when you need a known sequence of numbers or index positions.
concepts: len(sequence) returns how many items it holds
range stops before its end value
range(len(party)) yields valid indexes; range(1, len(party) + 1) yields human numbers

examples.title: Party size and human numbers
examples.code:
party = ["Mara", "Tovin", "Sable"]
print(len(party))

for number in range(1, len(party) + 1):
    print(number)
examples.explanation: len returns 3. range(1, 4) yields 1, 2, 3 — the stop value is not produced.

examples.title: Index plus name
examples.explanation: Indexes 0, 1, and 2 pair with each name in order.

common_mistakes: Confusing item count with the last valid index
Treating a string as one item instead of a sequence of characters

exercises.title: Stop before the stop
exercises.prompt: What does this print? Type each line of output.
exercises.failure_message: The second number passed to range is the stopping boundary; it is not produced.
hints: range starts at the first argument and stops before the second.
The values are 1, then 2, then 3 — not 4.

exercises.title: Count or final index?
exercises.prompt: What does this print? Type each line of output.
hints: len(party) counts how many names are in the list.
The last valid index is one less than the length.
First line is 3; second line is the final name, Sable.

exercises.title: The missing final member
exercises.prompt: The roster stops before Sable. Fix the range() call without changing the list or print line.
hints: range already stops before its ending number.
len(party) is 3, which generates the valid indexes 0, 1, and 2.

tests.message: Keep range(...) as the sequence driving the for loop.
Keep the for loop that walks indexes.

exercises.title: Numbered roster
exercises.prompt:
Write numbered_roster(party) that returns a list of strings, one per member, in this exact format:
1: Mara
2: Tovin
3: Sable

Use a for loop and range. Do not hardcode names or positions. Return the list of formatted lines (do not print them).
hints: Human numbers run from 1 to len(party); indexes run from 0.
Loop with range and build each line from the number and party[index].
Collect f"{number}: {party[index]}" strings in a list and return that list.

tests.message: Inside numbered_roster, use range(...) as the for-loop sequence.
Use a for loop with range to build the roster lines.

tests.name: party
tests.message: Read each name with party[index], not a hardcoded string.

exercises.title: Name length
exercises.prompt: Write is_long_name(name) returning True when a name contains 8 or more characters.
hints: len works on strings as well as lists.

tests.message: Inside is_long_name, measure the name with len(name).
